rv.q: This magnificent revival of Arthur Miller’s study of real and allegorical witch hunts has grown in stature since it opened at the National Theatre nine months ago.
The entire production has an eerie, engulfing quality thanks to Es Devlin’s picture-perfect diorama of a set.
A magnificent revival, with a strong ensemble.
‘The Crucible’ is not just a moral tale. In contrast with the story of good people being destroyed by lies and religious fanaticism, there is also the portrait of a troubled marriage
This production of The Crucible is well worth seeing, even if it’s a play you know as well as John Proctor knows his own name.
It's a watchable production of a great play, but it could have been so much more.
The play demands a powerful chemistry between them, but this is sadly lacking in their performance.

The staging, the direction, the production elements and indeed the cast makes ‘The Crucible’ a show that impresses on all fronts and is a fitting addition to the legacy of Arthur Millers classic. I have reached my verdict and my judgement is that this show really is devilishly good.

While certain aspects of this show ring true, it’s a shame that the production as a whole lacks enough emphasis on these to create a whole show worth revisiting. It’s one we are glad to have seen and will still sit with us yet there is definitely more untapped potential in the source material for the creative team to uncover here.

cn.t: Lyndsey Turner's spellbinding revival of Miller's classic earns strong praise for its intensity and claustrophobic staging, with critics calling it "magnificent." Some question symbolic choices, but the production's power largely captivates.
